claims.text: The initial material is a rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The initial alloy is primarily a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Isothermal aging at 300°C will promote precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The precipitation induced by aging is diffusion-driven.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds will preferentially precipitate along grain boundaries.
During aging, the metastable solid solution decomposes through Mg diffusion, localized segregation, and precipitation.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates alter the local chemical potential during subsequent oxidation.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites for MgO at precipitate–matrix interfaces.
Precipitation promotes formation of a contiguous, coherent, and adherent MgO scale during oxidation at 500°C.
The MgO scale is protective.
The precipitation-mediated oxide scale changes the alloy's high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
The precipitation-mediated oxide scale improves corrosion resistance relative to the as-quenched baseline.
Aged samples will have a greater volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics than the as-quenched sample.
Aged samples will form a more uniform MgO scale than the as-quenched sample during subsequent oxidation.
Samples are to be aged in air at 300°C for 1, 5, or 10 hours and compared with an as-quenched control.
All samples are to undergo oxidation at 500°C for 5 hours before standardized corrosion testing.
Microgalvanic interactions associated with increased intermetallic formation may counteract the proposed protective effect and worsen corrosion.
Alternative transformation mechanisms may operate outside the specified aging and oxidation temperature regimes.

The hypothesis is falsified if aging does not significantly increase intermetallic formation or change oxide morphology, or if increased intermetallic formation is accompanied by deteriorated corrosion performance.
